questions.q: What is the difference between `-p 8080:3000` and `-P` on `docker run`?
options: They do exactly the same thing
-p maps a specific host port to a specific container port; -P publishes every EXPOSEd port to a random free host port each time
-P only works with official images
-p requires the container to already be running
questions.explain: -p gives you a predictable, specific mapping. -P publishes all ports the image's Dockerfile marked with EXPOSE, but to a different random host port on each run.

questions.q: Why would Northbridge use `--env-file` instead of multiple `-e` flags for the checkout service?
options: --env-file is required for any container with more than one port
Checkout needs a dozen variables, and one file is easier to review and version than a growing pile of -e flags
-e flags are deprecated and no longer work in current Docker versions
--env-file makes the container start faster
questions.explain: --env-file loads every KEY=value line from a file into the container's environment at startup -- practical once you have more than a couple of variables to manage.

questions.q: What does `docker logs -f catalog` do differently from plain `docker logs catalog`?
options: It deletes old log entries before showing new ones
It follows the log stream live, printing new lines as they're written, instead of just printing what's already there and exiting
It forces the container to restart before showing logs
It filters logs to only show error-level messages
questions.explain: -f (follow) keeps the log stream open so new output appears as the container produces it, rather than showing a single snapshot.

questions.q: What does `docker port checkout` show you?
options: The CPU and memory usage of the checkout container
Which host ports the checkout container's exposed ports were actually mapped to
A list of all environment variables set on the checkout container
The checkout container's full startup log
questions.explain: docker port lists the actual host-port mappings for a container's published ports -- especially useful after -P, since the host port is chosen randomly.

questions.q: What's the first thing an on-call engineer typically checks when a running container starts behaving oddly?
options: docker rm -f to remove the container immediately
docker logs -f to watch what the container is writing to stdout/stderr in real time
docker pull to download a fresh copy of the image
docker pause to freeze the container permanently
questions.explain: Watching live log output is usually the fastest, lowest-risk way to see what a misbehaving container is actually doing, before reaching for heavier debugging tools.
